articles.title: Multas por excesso de velocidade crescem 32% na cidade de SP em 2026 | G1
articles.standfirst: Quase 9 em cada 10 autuações foram de motoristas que trafegavam até 20% acima do limite. Especialistas apontam distração, uso do celular e tentativa de compensar o tempo perdido no trânsito entre fatores que podem explicar o comportamento.
articles.summary: Quase 9 em cada 10 autuações foram de motoristas que trafegavam até 20% acima do limite. Especialistas apontam distração, uso do celular e tentativa de compensar o tempo perdido no trânsito entre fatores que podem explicar o comportamento.
articles.body:
Avenida Prestes Maia, no Centro de São Paulo, está entre as vias com mais multas por excesso de velocidade — Foto: Reprodução/TV Globo

O número de multas por excesso de velocidade aumentou 32,5% na cidade de São Paulo nos cinco primeiros meses de 2026 , na comparação com o mesmo período do ano passado.

Dados do Observatório Mobilidade Segura, da Prefeitura de São Paulo, mostram que foram aplicadas 1.377.415 multas entre janeiro e maio de 2026, contra 1.039.207 no mesmo período de 2025.

Apesar do aumento, a grande maioria das infrações deste ano não envolve motoristas flagrados muito acima do limite da via: 88,48% das multas foram aplicadas a veículos que trafegavam até 20% acima da velocidade permitida .

Outros 10,38% foram flagrados entre 20% e 50% acima do limite. Apenas 1,14% das infrações foram registradas por velocidade superior a 50% da máxima permitida – tipo de infração que leva à perda da habilitação, além da multa gravíssima.

Distração é um dos principais fatores para multas

Para o arquiteto e urbanista Flamínio Fichmann, assessor técnico do Instituto de Engenharia, a distração é um dos fatores que ajudam a entender o comportamento dos motoristas.

"As pessoas estão cada vez mais distraídas por uma série de motivos. Na conjuntura de quem mora nas grandes cidades, a pressão em função das suas obrigações, dos seus compromissos, está cada vez maior. Então existe um estresse em relação a isso, e as pessoas estão mais distraídas. E o motivo principal dessa distração, eu não tenho dúvida, é o uso de celular."

Outra possível explicação apontada pelo especialista está na própria dinâmica do trânsito paulistano. Depois de enfrentar congestionamentos, alguns motoristas podem acelerar quando encontram trechos mais livres.

"As pessoas, quando pegam um trânsito mais intenso em determinado trecho, em determinado horário, muitas vezes podem tentar compensar em outros horários, em outros trechos."

Multas por excesso de velocidade crescem 32% em São Paulo em 2026 — Foto: Reprodução/TV Globo

De acordo com o especialista, o aumento de autuações registrado este ano pode estar relacionado à maior circulação de veículos individuais.

"Existe um congestionamento maior na cidade. Exatamente pela redução do uso de transporte público, a gente vem assistindo a uma participação menor do transporte público e a uma participação maior do transporte individual. Devido a essa proporção maior do transporte individual, a gente percebe que existem mais pessoas circulando e mais expostas a situações vinculadas à regulamentação de velocidade."

Os dados de maio de 2026, mês mais recente com registros disponíveis, mostram que domingo é o dia da semana com a maior concentração de multas por excesso de velocidade : 20,8% do total.

Na sequência aparecem sábado (17,3%), sexta-feira (15,2%), segunda-feira (13,3%), terça-feira (11,8%), quarta-feira (10,9%) e quinta-feira (10,7%).

Ou seja, mais de um terço das multas costumam ocorrer aos finais de semana .

Especialistas apontam que distração está entre fatores que mais levam motoristas a trafegarem com velocidade acima do permitido — Foto: Reprodução/TV Globo

A distribuição das infrações por horário também mostra que a maior parte dos flagrantes de velocidade acima do permitido acontece durante o dia .

Em maio, 30,9% das multas foram registradas entre 12h e 17h59, e outros 30,3%, entre 6h e 11h59. Juntas, as duas faixas representam 61,2% das autuações.

Entre 18h e 23h59 foram registradas 20,4% das multas. A madrugada, entre 0h e 5h59, respondeu por 18,4%.

Entre os locais com maior número de multas aplicadas pela CET (Companhia de Engenharia de Tráfego) por excesso de velocidade estão pontos da Avenida Prestes Maia (Centro), Radial Leste, Avenida Jacu Pêssego (Zona Leste) e Avenida Olavo Fontoura (Zona Norte).

O Código de Trânsito Brasileiro divide o excesso de velocidade em três categorias.

Quem circula até 20% acima da velocidade máxima permitida comete infração média . Segundo a CET, são quatro pontos na carteira e multa de R$ 130,16.

Quando a velocidade fica mais de 20% e até 50% acima do permitido, a infração é grave , com cinco pontos e multa de R$ 195,23.

Já dirigir mais de 50% acima da velocidade máxima é infração gravíssima . O valor informado pela CET é de R$ 880,41, devido à aplicação do fator multiplicador de três, e há suspensão direta do direito de dirigir.

Em nota, a CET afirmou que a quantidade de multas aplicadas "reflete diretamente o comportamento dos condutores que desrespeitam as leis de trânsito estabelecidas pelo Código Brasileiro de Trânsito (CTB)".

A companhia ressaltou que os radares apenas registram as infrações e afirmou que São Paulo mantém praticamente a mesma quantidade de pontos de fiscalização eletrônica desde 2014.

articles.title: Pedestres relatam dificuldade para atravessar rodovia em Piracicaba | G1
articles.standfirst: Segundo moradores, acidentes são frequentes no local, mas poderiam ser evitados com a instalação de uma passarela para travessia. Caso ganhou repercussão após engavetamento nesta quinta-feira (8).
articles.summary: Segundo moradores, acidentes são frequentes no local.
articles.body:
Pedestres que passam pelo Km 167 da Rodovia Geraldo de Barros, em Piracicaba (SP), tem reclamado da dificuldade para travessar a via e pedem a instalação de uma passarela no trecho.

A região tem um grande fluxo de pedestres, devido a um supermercado e um ponto de ônibus localizados no local.

Jorge da Silva utiliza o ponto frequentemente e conta que o local sempre é cenário de acidentes e que isso poderia ser evitado caso houvesse uma estrutura para travessia adequada.

"É difícil, já morreu uns par de pessoas e é o seguinte, aqui não tem projeto. Eu conheço Piracicaba mais de 40 anos. Sempre estou comentando sobre isso aqui. Já era para ter uma passarela faz tempo."

Pedestres relatam dificuldade para atravessar a Rodovia Geraldo de Barros em Piracicaba — Foto: Edjan del Santo/EPTV

A aposentada Margarida dos santos Paulo diz que a passarela já é solicitada pelos cidadãos há muito tempo, porém nada foi feito.

"Aqui é um desastre, um desastre. A gente já fez muito abaixo-assinado, mas nada resolve. E muitas mortes já teve aqui."

Em nota, o Departamento de Estradas de Rodagem (DER) informou que existe um contrato para implantação de passarela no local e que as obras serão iniciadas o mais rápido possível. Confira abaixo:

"O DER-SP informa que há um contrato para implantação de passarela no km 167 da Rodovia Luiz de Queiróz (SP 304), em Piracicaba, atualmente em processo de atualização do projeto executivo, para viabilizar a execução dos serviços no menor prazo possível, seguindo os trâmites legais e administrativos previstos."

Segundo o DER, o trecho está em condições adequadas, devidamente sinalizado, com faixas redutoras de velocidade e faixa para travessia de pedestres.

Motoristas pararem para os pedestres atravessarem na faixa em locais sem semáforo é lei no Brasil, de acordo com o Código de Trânsito Brasileiro.

Porém, de acordo com os pedestres que passam no local, a maioria dos motoristas não respeita essa regra. Isso obriga que passa ali a esperar um longo período para realizar a travessia.

"Demora meia hora, 20 minutos para passar aqui. Vários acidentes já aconteceram'', conta Célio Almeira.

No ponto, o local mais seguro para atravessar é em um semáforo localizado a cerca de 1 km, pois lá a parada dos veículos é obrigatório. Porém a distância torna a alternativa impraticável para idosos e pessoas com mobilidade reduzida, por exemplo.

"É horrível, principalmente para os idosos, mãe com criança. É assim, se você não se arriscar, você acaba ficando para trás. Ano passado, uma idosa foi acidentada aqui. E hoje ela nem pega mais ônibus aqui, porque ela pegou trauma", explica Gislaine Rodrigues Ferreira, que utiliza o ponto.

Outro pedestre conta que a falta de uma passarela apresenta riscos também paras os motoristas, que podem se envolver em acidentes.

No caso de quinta-feira, os carros bateram pois um dos veículos parou para possibilitar a travessia de uma pessoa, porém os veículos que vinham atrás não pararam a tempo.

"Aqui virou uma roleta russa. Se você for atravessar na faixa, é perigoso alguém parar e acontecer outro engavetamento. Nós estamos aguardando a providência das promessas das autoridades, mas até agora nada", relata Paulo Roberto.

Engavetamento entre sete carros bloqueia parcialmente Rodovia em Piracicaba — Foto: Edjan del Santo/EPTV

articles.title: Wall Street Sees an Ominous Sign in Bond Market’s Latest Selloff
articles.summary: It’s one of the least understood signals in the fixed-income world, but lately, everyone on Wall Street is abuzz about what it means as it reasserts itself i...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- It's one of the least understood signals in the fixed-income world, but lately, everyone on Wall Street is abuzz about what it means as it reasserts itself in the market.

It's known as the term premium, or the extra payout that investors demand in return for the risks of owning 10-year Treasuries instead of just rolling over short-dated securities for the same amount of time. How exactly to measure it varies. So do the explanations for its moves.

What's not in question is that during the past few weeks it spiked to levels not seen in over a decade and drove the latest leg of the bond selloff that's sent US Treasury yields to a 24-year high. And that, in turn, is fanning fears of a potential shift that will heap pressure on an already battered market and keep borrowing costs elevated across the economy.

That term premium is essentially protection against unpredictable turns, ranging from geopolitical shocks to government fiscal crises, that could hit the market before long-term bonds come due.

It's distinct from the current outlook for inflation and the direction of monetary policy, both of which are also reflected in yields. Because the premium isn't directly observable and must be inferred, Neel Kashkari, the president of the Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis, once likened it to dark matter, the invisible substance physicists say explains some cosmic mysteries.

"There's multiple ways to calculate it, but they're all going higher," said Frank Rybinski, head of macro strategy at Aegon Asset Management. "And what that tells me is that this move has staying power."

"The sharp repricing of term premium embedded in Treasuries — with 10-year term premium breaking out to a 12-year high — suggests investors are demanding greater compensation for holding duration amid mounting fiscal and geopolitical uncertainty."

There was no clear-cut catalyst. Barclays researchers led by Demi Hu said macroeconomic uncertainty, breakdowns in the usual correlations between stock and bond moves, the rising supply of debt and worries about fiscal policy are all things that figure into the term premium and could be playing a role.

articles.title: Trump slashes tariffs to flood U.S. with 661 million pounds of foreign beef — Nebraska ranchers push back
articles.summary: Beef prices hit $6.92 per pound as Trump cuts tariffs on Brazilian and Argentine imports, angering U.S. ranchers.
articles.body:
In March 2026, President Donald Trump touted the value of American beef , saying he wanted to make it easier for Americans to buy U.S.-made beef. But in recent months, his administration has clashed with ranches and farms extensively.

Beef prices in the U.S. have skyrocketed from an average of $4.47 per pound in August 2021 to $6.92 in August 2026.

The tax breaks in Trump's 'big beautiful bill' expire after 2028. Here are 4 moves to make before the window closes

Jeff Bezos backs a platform that lets anyone invest in rental homes for as little as $100 — 6 ways to build wealth like a landlord without actually being one

Dave Ramsey warns nearly 50% of Americans are making 1 big Social Security mistake. Here's what it is and 3 simple steps to fix it ASAP

The Trump administration has responded by drastically cutting tariffs on imported beef , allowing 300,000 metric tons — or 661 million pounds — into the U.S. It promises the beef will be sold at 25% below market prices.

That might seem reassuring next time you're at the grocery store, but for food inspection experts and American ranchers , this has been a worrying development.

And for voters in Nebraska, where the cattle industry was worth $11.43 billion in 2025 , it could help sway a competitive House race to the left.

For ranchers across the U.S., it has been a dry, difficult year.

According to the U.S. Drought Monitor , 57% of American cattle are in locations with moderate or greater drought, a 27% year-over-year growth.

The total amount of cattle in the U.S. has been declining for decades, with 86 million heads of cattle at the start of 2026 . That leaves ranchers with a difficult decision : Do they focus on increasing the size of their herd, or do they improve short-term profits by selling cattle?

America's constrained beef supply is complicated by the fact that the government is heavily pushing beef as a health food.

That's largely due to the Make America Healthy Again (MAHA) movement, spearheaded by Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. On Jan. 11, 2026, the White House posted a photo of Kennedy on X with the caption "We are ending the war on protein."

Kennedy has extensively promoted beef, as well as beef tallow as a cooking fat. Doctors have raised concerns , saying that Kennedy is wrong about seed oils being dangerous and beef fat benign.

articles.title: Nobel Peace Prize Goes to International Jurist Navi Pillay
articles.summary: The 2026 Nobel Peace Prize was awarded to Navanethem “Navi” Pillay for her efforts to promote peace and international law.
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- The 2026 Nobel Peace Prize was awarded to Navanethem "Navi" Pillay for her efforts to promote peace and international law.

"The system of international law is under tremendous pressure, and its institutions are under attack," Jørgen Watne Frydnes, chair of the Norwegian Nobel Committee, told reporters. "We see a shift towards power politics at the expense of legal frameworks and global respect for law and justice."

The laureate will receive 12 million Swedish kronor ($1.2 million) in prize money, the Norwegian Nobel Committee in Oslo said in a statement on Friday.

"Navi Pillay is one of the great defenders of international legal principles in our time. Her distinguished career reminds us of the need to support, fortify and expand the global rule of law," Watne Frydnes said. Her "commitment to justice and human dignity is a source of hope and inspiration to all who seek to bring about a more peaceful world."

Pillay, 85, has served as a judge in South Africa, at the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda and the International Criminal Court. She was UN High Commissioner for Human Rights from 2008 to 2014 and later chaired the UN Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory.

Born into an Indian Tamil family in Durban, South Africa, Pillay founded her own law firm in 1967 and earned a doctorate from Harvard University in 1988.

"A common thread runs from her early work defending Nelson Mandela and others who stood up against apartheid to her service as a judge in some of the key international court cases of our time," the committee said.

Ahead of the award, there were wild swings in betting on the Polymarket platform, with Yulia Navalnaya, the widow of late Russian opposition leader Alexey Navalny emerging as the frontrunner overnight. An hour before the announcement, she was neck-and-neck with Mykola Kuleba, Ukrainian children's rights activist.

In 2025, a leak of Nobel Peace Prize laureate María Corina Machado's name triggered an unusual betting surge on the Polymarket platform hours before she was unveiled as the award recipient.

Arguably the most prestigious prize in global diplomacy, the Nobel Peace Prize can also stir controversy. Last year, Donald Trump campaigned aggressively, and ultimately unsuccessfully, to obtain the award, which he has long coveted. Earlier this year Machado gifted her medal to the US president, stunning Norway.

articles.title: GOP frustrates MAHA allies, risking midterm support from key voting bloc
articles.summary: “Make America Healthy Again” (MAHA) activists are growing frustrated with Republican leaders following a series of what many see as serious betrayals of the movement. The growing divide between the two comes just ahead of the midterm elections, where the GOP is already facing headwinds. The latest setback is the farm bill, supported by Republicans…
articles.body:
“Make America Healthy Again” (MAHA) activists are growing frustrated with Republican leaders following a series of what many see as serious betrayals of the movement .

The growing divide between the two comes just ahead of the midterm elections, where the GOP is already facing headwinds.

The latest setback is the farm bill, supported by Republicans purporting to be MAHA sympathizers. Activists are pushing back on the inclusion of a provision to delay a deadline for Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) pesticide safety reviews. They’re also raising concerns about cuts to certain conservation programs.

Meanwhile, Trump administration officials hobnobbing with key industries and little activist presence at a recent MAHA summit are also exacerbating tensions.

Voters in this bloc are characterized by their support for Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. as well as distrust of vaccine mandates and chemical and agriculture corporations. Activist Zen Honeycutt, founder of Moms Across America, warned that MAHA-aligned voters could sit out the midterms — meaning the potential loss of a key pocket of support for Republicans.

“Do we vote for someone who supports vaccine mandates … or do we vote for someone who is actively supporting pesticides and poison in our foods that our babies and children eat on a daily basis?” Honeycutt said. “It’s an impossible decision, and this is why many of our moms are saying they’re going to stay home, or vote independent, write somebody in.”

During last week’s summit, Kennedy and other administration officials mingled with executives from drug developers, AI companies, insurers and retailers like Walmart.

Some grassroots activists accused MAHA leaders of selling out to the corporate interests they pledged to fight.

Robert Malone, who previously was vice chair of Kennedy’s vaccine advisory committee, wrote a scathing blog titled “The Capture of MAHA.”

“The people who built this movement were promised an end to … Washington influence-peddling, not a MAHA-branded version of it,” he wrote.

In the farm bill , activists are raising particular concerns about a provision that would extend the deadline for the EPA to re-review health impacts of pesticides that are already on the market.

“Under law, you’re supposed to re-review pesticides every 15 years. That is to account for emerging science and complete what’s known as the registration review process to ensure that both people and the environment are being appropriately protected,” said J.W. Glass, senior EPA policy specialist at the Center for Biological Diversity.

For pesticides that were on the market prior to a 2007 update to the law, the deadline had previously been 2026. The farm bill would extend it to 2031.

Glass said that pushing the deadline back amounts to “kicking the can down the road and allowing EPA to not take a hard look at products that have been on the market now for … multi-decade intervals, and not have any sort of theoretical or legal deadline keeping them from moving forward.”

Citing that provision, activist Vani Hari called Republicans on the Senate Agriculture Committee, all of whom recently voted to advance the legislation, “MAHA Traitors” in a post on the social platform X .

Activist Kelly Ryerson said that pushing back the deadline “is just going to be even more harmful to human health” and said it could mean “another five-year break to glyphosate regulation.”

She additionally warned of cuts to certain conservation programs, raising concerns about funding for a regenerative agriculture pilot program.

According to the University of Illinois , the Senate Republican bill cuts nearly $2 billion from the Environmental Quality Incentives Program , which provides money to farmers for conservation.

Republicans defended their legislation, noting that the EPA has not been able to get all of the reviews done on time. They say their bill gives the EPA a more reasonable time to complete the process and that the extension would prevent lawsuits against the agency.

They also said there’s no overall cut to conservation programs, noting that conservation funds are instead being moved to support new Forest Conservation Easement and State Conservation Assistance programs. They also said the legislation does not forbid the regenerative agriculture program from moving forward.

A committee spokesperson said via email that the farm bill “was crafted with input from producers to deliver the programs and tools they need to meet today’s challenges and build a stronger, more resilient future for American agriculture.”

Ryerson, who goes by the moniker “Glyphosate Girl” online, directed some of her ire specifically at Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kan.), chair of the Senate MAHA Caucus and a member of the Agriculture Committee, who is facing a surprisingly tough fight to retain his seat.

She said MAHA- and Kennedy-aligned voters “should not be supporting Marshall and I think they should vote for the Democrat.”

Long-standing disagreements not going away

The tensions come on top of long-standing disagreements between Republicans and the movement, including on issues related to pesticides and chemicals, plus fights earlier this year about other pesticide provisions in the farm bill.

In a sign of further dissatisfaction with the GOP leaders, former Kennedy campaign adviser and MAHA advocate Tiffany Cianci issued a scorecard on Thursday accusing the Trump administration of breaking 85 percent of its promises to MAHA on agriculture, environment and food safety.

The scorecard cites issues including the appointment of chemical industry personnel at the EPA, actions to support pesticide companies including backing the industry in a key Supreme Court case, rollbacks to air and water regulations, cuts to the Food and Drug Administration and healthy food programs, and tariffs and other farm policies.

Jeff Hutt, who worked on Kennedy’s presidential campaign, agreed that many of the MAHA supporters who backed Trump in 2024 specifically because of Kennedy may stay home. Republicans shouldn’t count on those votes, he said, because the party is more beholden to Trump than to the MAHA ideals.

“The Republican Party really went from being a big tent party in ‘24 to a pup tent party in ‘26. I think a lot of those voters are going to stay home,” he said.

But Hutt added that the MAHA movement was never intended to be partisan, and the alignment with Republicans has always had an expiration date.

“If you look at the movement and you look at how it’s impacted politics, I think it’s been very successful,” Hutt said. “But I think if you look at it through the lens of a caucus within the Republican Party, I don’t think that has been very successful. But I really don’t think that that was very realistic from the get-go.”

articles.title: 16-year-old allegedly led ransomware gang behind hundreds of attacks
articles.summary: Operation KillSwitch dismantled KillSec's ransomware infrastructure, but investigators say a 16-year-old allegedly ran the entire cybercrime operation.
articles.body: When you picture the person running an international ransomware operation, a 16-year-old probably does not come to mind. Yet investigators say a teenager was the suspected main operator behind KillSec, a cybercrime group linked to around 1,000 suspected attacks worldwide. About 500 of those attacks have so far been identified as successful. Now, an international law enforcement operation has taken KillSec's leak site and key servers offline. Authorities also secured at least 110 terabytes of stolen data that could have been exposed or used to pressure victims. The takedown offers a remarkable look at how accessible cybercrime has become. More importantly, it shows how attackers continue to find their way into poorly protected systems and turn stolen files into leverage. What investigators uncovered about KillSec shows how the group operated, how AI reportedly played a role and what you can do to make ransomware attacks harder to pull off. Explore classes on stopping spam, phone security, financial protection and using AI to get better health care. Each class is free, easy to follow and comes with a free printable checklist. See the classes and register at CyberGuyLive.com. FBI STRIKES BACK AT HACKING GROUP WITH OVERSEAS ARREST OF ALLEGED LEADER Police take down KillSec ransomware operation The crackdown, known as Operation KillSwitch, took place on Sept. 30. Authorities from the United States and several European countries participated in the investigation. Europol and Eurojust also helped coordinate the effort. Police carried out eight searches in Greece, Romania, Spain and the United Kingdom. Three suspects were provisionally arrested. Investigators also took control of five central servers connected with KillSec's operation. One of the biggest moves involved KillSec's dark web leak site. The group allegedly used the site to name victims and threaten to publish stolen files unless they paid. Authorities have now taken control of that infrastructure. A 16-year-old is suspected of running the operation Perhaps the most startling part of this case involves the age of the suspected operator. Investigators identified a 16-year-old as KillSec's suspected administrator and main operator. Another suspected member, described as a developer, turned 18 in August and was reportedly still a minor when some of the alleged crimes occurred. Investigators also identified people suspected of serving as a negotiator and an affiliate. Authorities say the investigation remains ongoing. Age aside, the alleged operation was anything but small. KillSec has been active since around 2024. According to Europol, the group exploited software vulnerabilities and poorly secured access points to break into organizations. Attackers then copied sensitive internal files to systems they controlled. How KillSec allegedly pressured its victims Once attackers had the files, the pressure began. KillSec allegedly listed organizations on its dark web site and threatened to publish their stolen data if they refused to pay. In some cases, the stolen files were reportedly made available after victims declined to hand over a ransom. Europol says the group received substantial ransom payments from some attacks. That strategy shows how ransomware has changed over the years. Criminals do not always need to lock every file on a computer to create leverage. Stolen information itself can become the threat. If an attacker gets employee records, customer information or confidential business documents, the victim can face serious consequences even when backups work perfectly. KillSec reportedly used AI to support its attacks Investigators also uncovered another detail that caught my attention. Europol says members of KillSec used artificial intelligence to help build and maintain ransomware infrastructure and identify potential victims. That does not mean AI carried out the entire attack by itself. However, it shows how cybercriminals can use the same technology everyone else is experimenting with to speed up parts of their work. A teenager may no longer need to build every piece of an attack from scratch. Tools, stolen credentials, vulnerable systems and AI assistance can lower some of the barriers that once required deeper technical expertise. That should make all of us pay closer attention to basic security habits. FBI'S FIRST CYBER FUGITIVE ON TEN MOST WANTED LIST RETURNS TO US AFTER CAPTURE IN VENEZUELA What happens to KillSec now? The investigation remains active. Authorities are examining computers, servers and other seized evidence. Investigators are also following cryptocurrency and other alleged criminal proceeds. That evidence could uncover additional attacks, victims or people connected with the operation. Europol also cautions that the current number of successful attacks may change as investigators continue reviewing what they seized. For now, KillSec's core infrastructure has taken a significant hit. However, ransomware groups have a long history of disappearing, reorganizing and resurfacing under different names. That makes prevention especially important even after a major takedown. Why this ransomware takedown should get your attention KillSec appears to have focused mainly on organizations rather than individual home computer users. Still, the methods behind the attacks offer lessons that apply to everyone. Europol says the group exploited software vulnerabilities and poorly secured access points. Those are the same types of weaknesses security experts have warned about for years. An old router, forgotten account or unpatched computer can give attackers an opening. A compromised password can do the same. Once criminals gain access, they can steal information before anyone realizes something has gone wrong. So, while you probably cannot stop an international ransomware gang yourself, you can make your devices and accounts harder to break into. 7 ways to reduce your ransomware risk A few simple security habits can close some of the openings attackers commonly look for. 1) Install software and security updates Do not keep putting off updates on your computer, phone, browser and other connected devices. Security updates often fix vulnerabilities attackers already know how to exploit. CISA recommends regularly patching operating systems and software, especially on devices exposed to the internet. Turn on automatic updates when that option is available. 2) Use strong, unique passwords Using the same password across several accounts gives an attacker more opportunities if one login is exposed. Create a different password for each important account. A password manager can help generate and store strong credentials without forcing you to remember every one. You should also check whether passwords you already use have appeared in known data leaks. Your iPhone or Android phone may already have tools that can flag compromised passwords. HACKER CLAIMS 7.49M CUSTOMER RECORDS STOLEN FROM AMERICAN UTILITY COMPANY 3) Turn on two-factor authentication A stolen password becomes much less useful when your account requires another form of verification. Enable two-factor (2FA) or multifactor authentication on your email, financial accounts, cloud storage and other important services. When available, consider phishing-resistant options such as passkeys or security keys instead of relying only on text-message codes. 4) Keep an offline backup of important files Ransomware becomes far more painful when your only copy of a photo, document or financial record lives on the compromised device. Back up important files regularly. Consider keeping one copy in the cloud and another on an external drive. If you use an external drive, disconnect it when the backup finishes. Some ransomware can also target drives that remain connected to an infected computer. 5) Be careful with unexpected downloads and attachments A convincing email, fake update warning or malicious attachment can provide an attacker with a way into your computer. Avoid opening files you were not expecting. Instead of clicking an urgent update prompt from a webpage or email, open the app itself and check for updates there. If something feels unusual, stop before entering a password or running a downloaded file. 6) Use security software on your devices Strong antivirus software can help detect ransomware, malicious downloads and other threats before they spread. Keep the protection updated and run a full scan if your computer suddenly behaves differently, redirects your browser or shows unfamiliar programs. Security software will never replace safe habits. However, it can provide another opportunity to catch a threat before the damage grows. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android & iOS devices at Cyberguy.com. 7) Know what to do if ransomware hits If you see a ransom message or suddenly lose access to important files, disconnect the affected device from your network. Avoid plugging backup drives into the compromised computer until you know the device is clean. The FBI says it does not support paying ransomware demands because payment does not guarantee that your information will be restored. The agency also encourages victims to report ransomware incidents. You can file a report with the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center at IC3.gov or contact your local FBI field office. The FBI specifically directs ransomware victims to use those channels. One more thing: type IC3.gov directly into your browser. The FBI has warned that scammers have created fake IC3 websites, including lookalike pages that may appear in sponsored search results. Kurt's key takeaways The age of KillSec's suspected operator is going to grab the headlines, and I understand why. Sixteen is incredibly young to be accused of running an operation connected with this many attacks. What stays with me, though, is how familiar the alleged entry points sound. Vulnerable software and poorly protected access can still give criminals exactly the opening they need. That is why I keep coming back to the basics. Update your devices. Protect important accounts with more than a password. Keep a backup that an attacker cannot easily reach. You may never know which security step stopped an attack. That is far better than discovering which one you skipped after your files are already gone. If a 16-year-old can allegedly help run a ransomware operation tied to hundreds of successful attacks, do you think powerful hacking tools and AI are making cybercrime too easy to enter at a young age? articles.title: House Dem seeks inspector general investigation of HHS claims in DOGE lawsuits
articles.summary: A top House Democrat said he is concerned the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) provided incorrect or fraudulent information as part of ongoing lawsuits into the Department of Government Efficiency’s (DOGE) infiltration of government information systems and wants the agency’s inspector general to investigate. In a letter sent Friday and shared first with…
articles.body:
A top House Democrat said he is concerned the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) provided incorrect or fraudulent information as part of ongoing lawsuits into the Department of Government Efficiency ’s (DOGE) infiltration of government information systems and wants the agency’s inspector general to investigate.

In a letter sent Friday and shared first with The Hill, Rep. Bobby Scott (D-Va.), the ranking member on the House Education and Workforce Committee, asked the HHS Office of Inspector General to open an investigation “immediately” into the matter.

“I am deeply concerned about the possibility that the Department is providing false or inaccurate information in litigation,” Scott wrote.

His letter focused on the efforts of billionaire Elon Musk, who previously helmed DOGE , and the group’s employees — who were provided access to the federal government’s payment system in January 2025 — exposing sensitive personal data, such as social security numbers, taxpayer ID numbers, information on children, and home addresses, of tens of millions of Americans.

DOGE officials also gained access to payment and contracting systems across the HHS that control hundreds of billions of dollars in annual payments to healthcare providers.

That data access and protection of the agency sparked a flurry of litigation from labor unions and other privacy advocates.

Scott said his concern stems from the HHS’s refusal to cooperate with an independent probe from the Government Accountability Office (GAO). He noted the agency denied the GAO’s request for a standard observational walkthrough of the department’s IT systems.

After the GAO submitted a modified request for artifacts and screenshots as verification, the health department again declined to cooperate. Scott said the HHS’s noncooperation stemmed from concerns that information, materials, items, or other documentation provided to the accountability office may not match those provided in litigation.

Scott also sent a letter to Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. in May asking for a detailed explanation about why the agency wasn’t cooperating with the investigation and what it meant by “discrepancies” between what the HHS produced in litigation and what it would provide to the GAO.

The Virginia Democrat said the department has not responded to numerous requests to “refute the assertion that it has provided misinformation to one or more courts.”

articles.title: Trump immigrant purge could cut social security for Americans by $2,000 a year
articles.summary: New report on economic cost of anti-immigration campaign projects 8.6% reduction in retirement payments by 2034
articles.body:
Elderly Americans can expect to lose an average of $2,152 in annual social security benefits each, a projected 8.6% reduction in their retirement payments, by 2034 and every year after as a direct consequence of the economic fallout from the Trump administration's anti-immigration campaign , if that carries on, according to a new report shared exclusively with the Guardian.

Already, US food prices are up, housing permits to build new homes are down – and even native-born Americans are losing out on potential jobs after the sudden exodus of 1.2 million foreign-born workers over the last two years as a result of Donald Trump's policies, the report finds.

"When the Trump administration says things, it's not always data-driven. And we wanted to see what the data shows, and what other people have found the data shows," said Michael Ettlinger, one of the report's authors. "Turns out that refutes what the US president primarily is asserting."

The blowback on the economy from Donald Trump's crackdown is wide-ranging, even as the federal government's aggressive mass deportation campaign quietly ramps up further .

"We are just beginning to see the harms in terms of what is happening here domestically. But the impacts of these policies, of these efforts, are going to be long-lasting. And I think that is by design," Vanessa Cárdenas, executive director of the pro-immigration reform organization America's Voice, told the Guardian.

The report, Economic Impacts of Trump Administration Immigration Policy, was commissioned by America's Voice and conducted by researchers at Economic Insights and Research Consulting, a firm focused on economic analysis.

Its conclusions underscore how recent federal policies revoking immigrants' legal protections or targeting them for enforcement have had dire effects on the nation's affordability crisis and job market, especially in regions and industries that rely disproportionately on foreign-born workers.

In the US agricultural sector, where 42% of crop workers are undocumented and 68% are foreign-born, farmers across the country are warning that the vast majority or in some cases all of their workforce has disappeared overnight, leaving produce to fall to, or rot in, the ground and go to waste .

Food products heavily reliant on immigrant labor have experienced much sharper price increases than food overall since Trump retook the White House, according to the report.

articles.title: Filling a bathtub with water before a hurricane? Why it’s common advice
articles.summary: If you’ve never experienced a hurricane, it may seem like odd advice.
articles.body:
(NEXSTAR) — For those who live in a hurricane-prone area, it may be second nature to fill your bathtub with water ahead of an impending storm. Outside of those regions, such a step may leave you confused .

As odd as it may sound to those who have never been through a hurricane, it is, indeed, listed in advice in nearly every hurricane preparedness guide, from the guide produced by Nexstar’s WFLA to FEMA’s hurricane prep sheet .

Not for drinking water, as you may have initially guessed, but instead for other bathroom-related purposes, like bathing and flushing the toilet — the latter of which could be crucial if you lose running water . It can also be used to clean surfaces and items.

Even before such a storm is in the forecast, experts recommend making sure your tub can hold water and, if you don’t have one, purchasing a drain stopper. You’ll want to act fast on the latter, as those often sell quickly .

If you’re preparing for a hurricane and don’t have a bathtub, you can fill other vessels, like buckets or plastic storage bins, with water for bathing, flushing the toilet, and cleaning.

These steps are for those who are not evacuating. It is also recommended that you have extra drinking water if you are staying in your home. If you plan to evacuate and come back after the storm has passed, you don’t need to fill your bathtub with water.

Other common preparation advice for those who may be impacted by a hurricane includes having a disaster supplies kit, installing storm shutters for your windows, setting refrigerators and freezers to maximum cold temperatures, and ensuring you have cash and a full tank of gas in your vehicle.

articles.title: Surveillance company Flock cuts staff as privacy backlash grows
articles.summary: Flock would not say if CEO Garrett Langley would take a pay cut following the reduction in workforce.
articles.body:
Surveillance camera maker Flock is cutting its workforce as the company faces ongoing and growing backlash to its license plate readers and people-tracking technology.

News of the staff cuts comes from Reuters, which reported that Flock is reducing its staff by 18%, or around 270 employees, across the board. The publication said the employees are leaving at the end of October following a voluntary buyout program.

Wired reported last month that Flock was asking some of its employees to leave, citing the need to shrink its staff to avoid mandatory layoffs.

Flock spokesperson Paris Lewbel told TechCrunch in a statement on Friday: “Flock recently offered current employees a generous Voluntary Separation Program as part of our efforts to position the company for its next phase of growth. This was a voluntary program, not a layoff, and reflects our continued focus on building a strong, sustainable business for the future.”

Flock’s spokesperson would not comment further when asked by TechCrunch if chief executive Garrett Langley or other executives took a pay cut as part of the program.

Flock has faced heavy criticism and mounting pushback from communities across the United States and legislators looking to rein in the company’s privately run mass surveillance program . Flock has installed over 100,000 license plate-reading cameras across the U.S., which allow police and federal agents to track the location and whereabouts of vehicles passing by them. Dozens of police officers have been arrested , fired, or forced to resign for abusing access to Flock’s system to search, track, and stalk people without a warrant or their permission.

While some cities have moved to take down Flock’s cameras citing public outcry, Flock quickly replaced them, prompting some Americans to destroy the cameras .

Flock has also been criticized for its poor cybersecurity, including allowing cameras to be publicly exposed and accessible from the web . Security experts have questioned Flock’s accuracy after the system has misidentified license plates, resulting in improper police stops and arrests, including a journalist who was driving an authorized review vehicle.

Several law enforcement departments, including Los Angeles’ police department , have allowed their contracts to expire or lapse, citing privacy and civil liberties concerns.

articles.title: Trump’s attempt to rename AI is looking awfully artificial
articles.summary: President Donald Trump has demanded “artificial intelligence” be renamed “super intelligence” and pushed the AI industry to get on board.
articles.body: President Donald Trump has a knack for turning words against his enemies. His first successful presidential run was built on monikers like “Little Marco” and “Crooked Hillary”; he changed “fake news” from a phrase describing scammy media outlets to a derogatory term for the press at large. Over the past few weeks, he’s clearly decided he can work the same magic to promote artificial intelligence — branding a technology he wants to accelerate “super”, while turning “artificial” into his latest go-to pejorative and declaring resisters “THE ENEMY.” Some of the biggest names in AI are going along with him. But he’s picked a tough linguistic battle, and it may not pan out the way he hopes. A longtime AI booster, Trump has gone into pro-robot overdrive since an industry conversation over “pacing” frontier development last month. His current position is that AI safety risks are overblown and US companies need to speed up development, including by building more data centers, which he insists contrary to polling data will be “very popular.” On top of discouraging industry self-regulation, he’s decided AI needs a rebrand by fiat. Trump declared in a rambling United Nations speech last month that “the use of the word artificial makes intelligence fake” and promised to rename the technology “super intelligence.” He then followed through with an executive order last week, forbidding the use of “AI” wherever possible. [Media: Changes have been swift. The US Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI), already a rebrand of the AI Safety Institute, has been renamed the Center for Advancing Innovation and Standards for Super Intelligence (CAISSI). Justice Department press releases have been modified to include the phrase, trumpeting that a man who flooded streaming platforms with AI-generated songs between 2017 and 2024 committed “Super Intelligence-Assisted Music Streaming Fraud.” On Thursday, Trump declared that “The White House considers anyone that uses the term, ‘Artificial Intelligence,’ as opposed to the highly accepted new and more accurate term, ‘Super Intelligence,’ THE ENEMY!” The same tech company figures who rushed to donate millions to Trump after his election have quickly signed on. Trump’s “First Buddy” Elon Musk has promised to rename SpaceXAI to SpaceXSI, while Jeff Bezos declared he likes it because “artificial is not a very flattering thing.” Jensen Huang, whom Trump called live on stage last month to rant that “robots will not be taking over,” has likewise adopted the term. Sam Altman praised it too, though he said OpenAI won’t be changing its name. As Trump tries to make SI happen, “artificial” is creeping into his vocabulary in the manner of earlier terms like “hoax” and “fake.” He recently announced that his long-favored epithet “fake news media” would be retired in favor of calling the press “artificial media,” and in an October 5th campaign rally (shortly before musing that Iran could “take out” Los Angeles and San Diego) he declared that concerns about war driving up prices were “just artificial.” As publicly happy as some AI industry figures have seemed with “SI”, Trump is functionally demanding a major industry rewrite its terminology. “Superintelligence” (one word) long predates Trump’s affection for “super”; it was popularized in an eponymous 2014 book by Nick Bostrom. But the term denotes highly advanced artificial intelligence that could surpass human thought, not the category of AI — an already nebulous term — as a whole. It’s one of several industry buzzwords (alongside artificial general intelligence and “useful general intelligence”) meant to define what comes after the current iteration of the tech. Trump adopting “super intelligence” might seem good for companies that had already hitched their wagon to superintelligence, including Meta and Microsoft. And as public opinion turns against AI, some in the industry may desire a rebrand. But forcing immediate adoption of SI also undercuts companies’ ability to promote big, new, flashy AI products as “superintelligent”, instead applying the term to everything from a future machine god to years-old music-slop generation tools. The field is even taking a downgrade with that additional corny space in the middle, since Trump’s attempts at earnestly good names have never really measured up to his insults. Meanwhile, Trump will have to convince the other branches of government to get on board with the term. He can’t bar Congress from using “artificial intelligence,” and it appears in existing laws like Trump’s signature Take It Down Act, which administration agencies will need to cite when arguing in court. As appetite for more AI regulation grows, congressional Republicans will have to decide whether to appease Trump by adopting a name many people find unintuitive, freighted with the baggage of Trump’s fairly unpopular pro-industry, anti-regulatory stance. And to make things even more confusing, pro-regulation figures like Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-VT) were already using the earlier definition of superintelligence in efforts to restrict powerful AI — Sanders cosponsored a bill called the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act in early September. Trump loves naming things, but his linguistic victories typically work when they’re catchy: either simple nicknames or distinctively funny turns of phrase. (Many people are saying!) “Super intelligence,” by contrast, simply comes off as a euphemism. A lot of Americans have tangible gripes with the industry, particularly around data centers, and insisting the tech is “super” does nothing to assuage these concerns. If anything, Trump’s escalating attempts to strong-arm people into a supposedly nicer term for AI makes him — and the industry itself — look awfully weak.

articles.title: Trump forms committee to investigate mortgage fraud allegations against Fed governor Lisa Cook
articles.summary: The president has tasked the committee with investigating whether Lisa Cook made false statements about two mortgages she took out.
articles.body:
President Trump has established a committee to investigate allegations against Federal Reserve governor Lisa Cook, including mortgage fraud and whether her statements constituted legal "cause" for Cook's removal from the central bank.

The president has tasked the committee with investigating whether Cook made false statements about two mortgages she took out. The group will report to him whether there is legal cause for Cook's removal.

Trump fired Cook, the first Black woman to serve as a Fed governor, in August 2025, claiming she committed mortgage fraud by making misrepresentations on loan documents years before her appointment to the central bank. Cook, a Biden appointee, has denied any wrongdoing and sued. The lawsuit has gone through multiple court rungs before reaching the Supreme Court earlier this year.

The Supreme Court ruled in June that Cook can continue serving on the Fed's Board of Governors, but did not rule on the merits of mortgage fraud allegations.

Section 10 of the Federal Reserve Act states that each member of the board shall hold office for 14 years unless sooner removed for cause by the president. The statute does not detail what constitutes "for cause." That term has been interpreted in legal rulings to mean inefficiency, neglect of duty, or malfeasance.

In a memo released Friday , the president instructed the committee to conduct an in-person hearing on Nov. 5 to consider the evidence and allegations against Cook. The hearing is set to take place at the White House.

"We have grave doubts that this 'hearing' is a legitimate one that would conform to the law," Abbe Lowell and Norm Eisen, lawyers representing Cook, said in a statement. "But if it is anything close to objective, the conclusion will be that Governor Cook did not commit mortgage fraud, leaving no cause to remove her from the Federal Reserve Board."

Cook's lawyers said they have engaged with the White House to evaluate whether the proposed process is genuine and not simply a "box-checking exercise."

The memo states that Cook may submit a written position statement to the committee regarding the allegations at least three days before the hearing and a post-hearing written statement by Nov. 10.

"As soon as practicable after receipt of that statement, the Committee shall submit written findings of fact and conclusions of law to me and shall recommend whether there is cause to remove Governor Cook from her position on the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve," Trump's memo states.

The assistant to the president for economic policy, the chair of the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, and the director of the Office of Government Ethics will serve as members of the committee.

articles.title: Leading Catholic bishop urges Pentagon against livestreaming execution
articles.summary: The president of the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops spoke out Friday against the Defense Department’s plan to livestream a firing squad execution next month. Archbishop Paul Coakley said he felt “shock and sorrow” when he learned of the plan to livestream the execution of former Army Maj. Nidal Hasan, who shot and killed 13…
articles.body:
The president of the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops spoke out Friday against the Defense Department’s plan to livestream a firing squad execution next month.

Archbishop Paul Coakley said he felt “shock and sorrow” when he learned of the plan to livestream the execution of former Army Maj. Nidal Hasan, who shot and killed 13 people at Fort Hood in Texas in 2009. A Pentagon official told The Hill that the military execution, the first in more than 60 years and the first by firing squad since World War II, will be livestreamed .

“In no way can Hasan’s actions be condoned, but this decision is a barbaric promotion of a culture of death and must be reconsidered,” Coakley said.

Coakley cited the biblical teaching not to “repay anyone evil for evil” and said a public execution will “undermine the moral fabric” of the nation. He said the execution would be a “blight on the conscience” of the American people.

“I pray for the intercession of Our Lady of Good Counsel that we as a nation may always choose life even in the most trying times and circumstances,” Coakley said.

Hasan carried out the deadliest shooting ever on a U.S. military installation. During his trial, in which he represented himself, Hasan said he “switched sides” and committed the shooting “in response to the U.S. wars in Iraq and Afghanistan.”

The shooter was found guilty in 2013 of 45 counts of premeditated and attempted premeditated murder. His case was tied up in the appeals process until the Supreme Court denied his final petition in 2025.

The decision to stream the military execution of Hasan has been met with criticism from both sides of the aisle. Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) slammed the decision as “beyond disgusting.”

“Public executions are what oppressive dictatorships like Iran and Afghanistan do,” Tillis wrote on social platform X . “It should not be happening in America.”

Sen. Chris Murphy (D-Conn.) also called the decision to livestream the killing “disgusting” and suggested Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth could be mimicking ISIS-style executions.

“I understand that in this country we have the death penalty, but public execution is medieval,” Murphy said in an appearance on CNN’s “Erin Burnett OutFront.”

Hegseth told The Hill that the victims and survivors “deserve justice without delays.” President Trump signed off on Hegseth’s recommendation of death by firing squad, which will happen at Fort Hood on Dec. 3.

articles.title: Frances Haugen hopes The Social Reckoning will inspire more whistleblowers
articles.summary: Facebook whistleblower Frances Haugen reflects on the portrayal of her story in Aaron Sorkin’s The Social Reckoning and her impact five years after going public.
articles.body: Facebook whistleblower Frances Haugen was mostly unfazed watching Oscar-winning actress Mikey Madison play a character named after her in The Social Reckoning, except for one thing: the wrist warmers. In Aaron Sorkin’s new thriller, the fictional Haugen — who, like her nonfictional counterpart, leaks thousands of documents to Wall Street Journal reporter Jeff Horwitz — habitually dons the accessories. It’s a character quirk that reflects real life, where they’re a way to deal with the effects of a vasoconstrictive disorder. “I’ve figured out lots of ways to minimize how much of an obstruction this is,” she tells The Verge in an interview. “But having to watch myself wear wrist warmers for two hours, I came out of it being like, ‘Oh my god, this is really disruptive. Like, how have I successfully not thought about this for like seven years?’” With The Social Reckoning appearing in theaters Friday, Haugen hopes Meta’s CEO might watch it and have a similar moment of recognition with his own counterpart: a callous, robotic character played by Jeremy Strong. “I hope Mark Zuckerberg watches the movie and has as much of a knee-jerk emotional response as I had on that regarding, ‘Do I really want to live this life anymore?’” Strong’s version of Zuckerberg has become sick of taking criticism for content moderation and fact-checking decisions as he prepares for congressional testimony, and waves off concern for design choices that his staff believe will stoke anger on the platform. “It’s very possible that Mark has learned to not see how distorted his world has become,” Haugen says. “My hope is that holding that mirror up, if he does ever watch the movie, that it gives him the gift of perspective, so he at least has a chance to choose.” Five years since she went public as the figure behind the Journal’s Facebook Files, Haugen hopes that the film can remind viewers about the breadth of information they uncovered and “humanize the whistleblowing experience.” While she says her mother may take issue with Madison’s young, brunette character being shorter and less blonde, she’s happy the fictional Haugen stands apart from her. “We want as many people as possible to see themselves in Mikey’s character,” she says. If someone at a frontier AI lab becomes “so unlucky that they find themselves in a place where they need to blow the whistle,” she hopes they’ll connect with the fictional Haugen and “be like, ‘Oh, I actually have a duty to my common human beings and fellow citizens to do that.’” One of Haugen’s most tangible impacts was providing evidence in lawsuits that claim Meta harmed young users, culminating in a $17 billion settlement earlier this year. But as the movie reminds viewers, child safety wasn’t what initially motivated her. In fact, documents about Instagram’s impact on teens were among the last she collected before resigning, because she worried clicking around too far outside her own subject area of civic integrity would raise alarms. “The collective memory of ‘What exactly was I complaining about?’ has shifted,” Haugen says. “Only about 10 percent of what I brought out was about kids.” Revelations about how the algorithm pushed users toward extremist groups, special content moderation privileges for elite users, and other issues “kind of disappeared into time,” she says. Meta declined to comment on the movie but has previously said the documents Haugen disclosed were cherry-picked and flatten decisions the company has had to make amid difficult tradeoffs. Still, Haugen has since engaged frequently on policy around social media and kids, much of that in Europe and Australia, where movement seemed more likely than in the US. While she says she’s “not a prohibitionist” when it comes to social media, she believes Australia’s youth social media ban pushed Meta to implement what she calls “‘yeah, duh’ features” to combat the threat. “I don’t think the first line of defense is you ban kids off social media,” she says. “But the problem is that platforms have shown repeatedly that they’re not particularly interested in making these spaces safe for kids, and Facebook particularly has shown they only improve safety for kids when they’re scared.” Meta has aggressively moved to silence another recent whistleblower, former public policy director Sarah Wynn-Williams, taking legal action to stop her from promoting her memoir about her time at the company, Careless People. But Haugen says she sees Meta’s action against Wynn-Williams as an “outlier,” in part because her retelling relied much more on personal narrative than Haugen’s reams of documents. Before Haugen’s character obtains the documents, “there’s a scene in the movie where the Jeff character tells the Frances character, ‘You didn’t give me evidence, you gave me a story,’” she says. “And because a lot of what [Wynn-Williams] is saying is dependent on her personal credibility, Meta very, very desperately needs no one else who had access to that same information to ever come forward.” As hype over artificial intelligence overtakes Meta and the rest of Silicon Valley, Haugen says conversations around industry regulation and public dissent are already much further along in AI than they were at a similar point with social media. Though she says some proposals seem “simplistic or misdirected,” like a pause on development, she’s encouraged that “we see people engaging, and we did not see people even engaging four years into social media.” Reflecting on her own decision to go public as a whistleblower, Haugen tells The Verge that she took a pretty dispassionate approach. She knew Meta could cause financial hurt, but says she didn’t worry too much about that. “I’m a Quaker and I don’t take a lot to be very content and happy,” Haugen says. “They can only take as much from you as you let them.”

articles.title: Billy Joel's Social Security Check vs. the Average American's
articles.summary: Even millionaires collect Social Security. Billy Joel’s likely benefit highlights an important retirement planning lesson.
articles.body:
You may think a wealthy guy like Billy Joel doesn't bother with Social Security, and well… you may be right.

Of course, the odds are the Piano Man, who would qualify at age 77, does collect a monthly check. Most celebrities, big shots, uptown girls and other wealthy folks do, even if they don't need the monthly income as much as your average joe(l).

Social Security isn't needs-based, so wealth doesn't disqualify anyone. As long as you've earned the required 40 work credits, as many celebrities do early in their careers, you're entitled to a monthly check. While a star musician or movie actor may not need the income, most still collect it because they paid into the system just like everyone else. It ain't no crime.

Let's assume the entertainer has earned the required work credits and has reported everything properly to the IRS. We do know that Mr. Joel owed millions in back taxes at one point, but it apparently wasn't his fault — an ex-manager allegedly created the issue by siphoning money for himself and otherwise mismanaging the star's finances, per coverage from People . Joel and the ex-manager eventually reached a settlement, but details were never shared with the public.

To hear Billy tell it, he was an innocent man.

Assuming all of that is true, how huge of a Social Security check would a superstar like Billy Joel bring in each month?

The figure may not be as high as you think. Yes, Social Security payments are calculated based on a person's income, and Billy Joel has a massive income from record sales, royalties and high-grossing concerts. He rakes in millions a year, and his net worth has been estimated at $250 million, according to publications like Social Life Magazine . He sold a Florida mansion for $42.6 million in 2024 and listed a Long Island estate for $49.9 million just this year, according to Realtor.com .

There is a cap on Social Security payouts, however. The maximum taxable earnings limit is currently $184,500 per year. With that, you can get the maximum payout allowed in 2026 — $5,181 per month. It's a reasonable bet that if Billy Joel does collect Social Security, the checks are in that neighborhood. It would depend in part on his age when he started collecting.

In other words, someone making $200,000 could qualify for the same Social Security payout as someone making $2 million, $20 million or more.

There's no need to go on and cry in your coffee for Mr. Joel or other well-heeled Americans — a monthly check for $5,181 is more than most people get. According to the Social Security Administration , the average retirement benefit is $1,976 a month.

Sen. Jon Ossoff (D) on Friday called Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth “a deeply unwell person” over his plan to livestream a firing squad execution next month.

“I think Pete Hegseth is, frankly … a deeply unwell person who seems to relish this kind of brutality,” Ossoff said on MS NOW.

The Pentagon a day prior revealed a surprise plan to livestream the Dec. 3 firing squad execution of the convicted Fort Hood, Texas, shooter, former Army Maj. Nidal Hasan, in what would be the military’s first execution in six decades. The plan immediately drew fierce blowback from both sides of the aisle, who have called the idea barbaric and below the country’s dignity and standards.

“Hasan should face the death penalty, but making his execution public and streaming it? Beyond disgusting,” Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.), wrote on the social platform X . “Public executions are what oppressive dictatorships like Iran and Afghanistan do. It should not be happening in America.”

Joe Kent, the former head of the National Counterterrorism Center who resigned in March over the Iran war, said streaming Hasan’s execution is “a stain on our morality” and “also gives the terrorists free propaganda that they will use to radicalize & recruit more terrorists like” Hasan.

Senate Armed Services Committee ranking member Jack Reed (D-R.I.) said in a statement that Hegseth’s plan is “a gift to anti-American terrorist recruiters” and is “absolutely shameful and damaging to America’s interests and core values.”

Hasan, a former Army psychiatrist, opened fire at Fort Hood in 2009, killing 13 people. He is set to be put to death on Dec. 3 at 1 p.m. local time at the same military base, according to Hegseth.

The last American service member to be killed by firing squad was Pvt. Edward Donald Slovik, who was convicted of deserting his unit twice in combat in France. He was executed in the country on Jan. 31, 1945.

“I kind of like the mentality we had in WWII, which was win, understand that when the enemy attacks you, you stand your ground,” Hegseth said Thursday.

Since then, the U.S. military has carried out only one other execution, with the 1961 hanging of Pvt. John Bennett for rape and attempted murder. The U.S. military has never in modern history made an execution public, and the last public execution of anyone in the U.S. was nearly a century ago in 1936.

Ossoff accused Hegseth of “spending his time with this kind of obscene medieval spectacle” rather than focusing on running the Pentagon, which he said is “falling into chaos.”

“The folks who are in positions of power in this administration, and of course we know all these things, but their values are in disarray, they’re totally disconnected from the daily experience of the American people, and their foreign policy is endangering the United States, squandering our international power and destroying our image in the world,” he said.

articles.title: Brendan Carr says he’ll let Pete Hegseth decide whether TV networks can air the public execution
articles.summary: FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said that he would defer to Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth on whether TV networks can air the planned execution of the Fort Hood shooter by firing squad, which the Pentagon says will be livestreamed.
articles.body: FCC chairman Brendan Carr said he will defer to Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth on whether TV networks can air the planned execution of convicted Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan by firing squad. The Pentagon has said the execution will be livestreamed, suggesting it’ll appear on an online platform beyond the FCC’s jurisdiction. But it’s common for broadcast TV networks to air live video of government events, and Carr’s agency does have a say over what happens on public airwaves. “My understanding is it’s not on broadcast TV, so I don’t think there’s a role for the FCC one way or the other,” Carr said in a CNBC interview today. “But I trust Secretary Hegseth. He’s implemented the laws and the regulations that are relevant to the Department of War, and I think he’s doing a great job, and I trust that he’s making the right call on these issues.” When asked if the execution would be allowed on broadcast TV if the Defense Department wanted it, Carr said it would be Hegseth’s choice. “Ultimately we’re going to defer to Secretary Hegseth and his decisions on how to move forward with this,” Carr said. The Verge has asked major tech companies whether they will allow the execution livestream on their platforms. As of this writing, YouTube, Twitch, Meta, and X haven’t responded to requests for comment.

articles.title: Russia will supply US and global markets with diesel, Trump says
articles.summary: Russia will supply the U.S. and global market with diesel, President Trump announced Friday, responding to sky-rocketing prices exacerbated by both the Russia-Ukraine and U.S.-Iran wars. The president’s move comes less than a month from the midterm elections, where rising energy prices are dominating voters’ concerns. Trump on Friday said that Russia would “immediately” supply…
articles.body:
Russia will supply the U.S. and global market with diesel, President Trump announced Friday, responding to sky-rocketing prices exacerbated by both the Russia-Ukraine and U.S.-Iran wars.

The president’s move comes less than a month from the midterm elections, where rising energy prices are dominating voters’ concerns.

Trump on Friday said that Russia would “immediately” supply 300,000 tons of diesel to the U.S. and the global marketplace.

“I have just concluded a highly successful discussion with President Vladimir Putin, of Russia, wherein it was agreed that Russia will immediately supply over 300,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel to the American and Global Marketplace, another 500,000 Tons during the month of November, and 1,000,000 Tons immediately thereafter,” he wrote in a post on Truth Social .

“Additionally, based on the condition of their Diesel Refineries, Russia will then deliver, within a short period of time, 3,000,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel,” he added.

Moscow confirmed its readiness to supply oil and petroleum to the U.S. and global markets, Putin said in a statement following the call reported by Russian state media .

Trump’s comments come after Russia banned diesel exports in the face of a shortage, with its energy production coming under attack from Ukrainian strikes. Late last month, the country had extended its ban until the end of October .

Ukrainian President Voldoymyr Zelensky rejected the U.S. move on Friday and said Ukrainian strikes are retaliation for Russia’s targeting of Ukraine’s energy infrastructure, in particular electrical grids, depriving people of light, heat and water.

“Ukraine is ready to take symmetrical de-escalatory steps, and the American team knows our position,” Zelensky said in a post on X . “Our strikes on Russian oil refineries and other oil facilities are a response to Russia’s years-long campaign of terror against Ukraine’s energy sector.”

The Treasury Department said Friday that it would be lifting sanctions on Russian diesel to allow the fuel into the global marketplace. A few weeks ago, Trump signed a bill into law that authorized further sanctions on Russia.

On Friday, the average diesel price in the U.S. was about $6.28 per gallon, up from about $3.68 a year ago, according to AAA .

On an average day, the U.S. transportation sector consumes about 2.94 million barrels of diesel.

Russia has historically been a major diesel exporter. A year ago, it was shipping about 2.5 million tons per month, but had been estimated to be shipping around 1 million metric tons in June, Reuters reported .

Andy Lipow, president of consulting firm Lipow Oil Associates, said he was “skeptical” that Russia would be able to come up with the promised barrels.

“I’m quite skeptical about those type of volumes being exported, given that currently Russia has imposed a diesel export ban in October,” Lipow told The Hill.

“Now, it’s certainly possible that once the harvest season ends in Russia, that we do see an increase in diesel exports, but I believe that Ukraine is going to continue to attack Russian refineries to impact on their ability to produce transportation fuels,” he said.

If Russia is able to come up with the barrels, Lipow said that the 300,000 ton and 500,000 ton figures are “quite small” compared to the entire global diesel market, though he said 3 million tons was more significant.

He says that if Russia does come up with the diesel to export, he expects there will be “some relief on diesel prices.”

Trump’s decision to facilitate Russian diesel on the market comes as he faces an Oct. 18 deadline to decide whether to impose sanctions targeting Russia’s energy industry or waive those authorities in the face of national security concerns.

The sanctions authorities are part of the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia Act, which Trump signed into law in September, concluding a more than year and a half long campaign to move forward the legislation. It was named for the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.), who died suddenly in July. Shortly before his death, Graham announced a breakthrough with the White House to move the bill forward.

A key part of the bill is Trump having authority to tariff countries that are the top five purchasers of Russian energy, largely taking aim at India and China.

The bill passed overwhelmingly in the Senate and drew a bipartisan majority in the House. Its supporters are likely to push back on Trump’s decision to ease pressure on Russia’s energy sector, viewed as the main financial engine supporting Putin’s war in Ukraine, now in its fourth year.

Zelensky, who hosted a bipartisan delegation of American lawmakers in Kyiv on Friday, said sanctions from the Graham bill must be imposed, pushing back on Trump’s announcement while saying that “Peace never comes through weakness.”

“There must be support for Ukraine in protecting lives, and there must be pressure on Russia for its war. And today, there was a conversation between the leaders of America and Russia. A conversation that leads to something different,” he posted on X .

Trump’s announcement also comes as Zelensky’s top officials for talks with Russia met in Miami with Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, who are leading U.S. negotiations between Moscow and Kyiv, Reuters reported .

articles.title: Southwest Airlines says ‘brief’ system outage affected boarding, checked bags
articles.summary: Southwest confirmed the news shortly after travelers began to report delays on Friday morning.
articles.body:
(NEXSTAR) – Southwest Airlines experienced a “brief” outage on Friday morning that affected the computer systems used to help check baggage and board flights.

Southwest confirmed the news shortly after travelers began to report delays.

“Southwest experienced a brief interruption due to a system outage at our vendor, Amadeus,” a spokesperson for the airline wrote in an emailed statement to Nexstar. “The airline continued to check baggage and board flights manually while full functionality was restored.”

The Amadeus IT Group, referenced in the statement, is a provider of travel software utilized by numerous global airlines.

“Amadeus briefly experienced a technical issue today affecting Southwest Airlines, originating from a third-party technology provider,” the IT company wrote. “Our teams took immediate action and worked closely with the provider to restore normal operations. We apologize for any inconvenience caused.”

Outage-detection platform DownDetector showed that passengers began reporting issues with Southwest shortly before 9 a.m., EDT on Friday.

Travelers claimed on social media that their gate agents were unable to scan their boarding passes , or that workers at the check-in gate were issuing handwritten baggage tickets. Others said they were told that all flights had been halted amid the outage, though the airline has disputed that was the case.

“[Flights were] not halted, just slowed due to manual processes,” a Southwest spokesperson said.

The airline’s initial statement also apologized to affected passengers.

We apologize to our Customers for any inconvenience and working to get them to their destinations as quickly as possible,” a spokesperson wrote. “Nothing is more important to Southwest than the Safety of our Customers and Employees.”
